Overview of the PEAS Model

The PEAS Model (Performance Measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors) is a foundational conceptual framework introduced by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig to formally define the task environment of a rational Artificial Intelligence agent. Before designing an agent program, system architects must explicitly specify the PEAS parameters, as the nature of the environment directly dictates the optimal agent architecture and decision-making algorithms required.

The four interconnected components of the PEAS framework are defined as follows:

  • Performance Measure: The objective, external metric used to evaluate how successful an agent's behavior is in achieving its goals. It quantifies the quality of environment states resulting from the agent's actions.
  • Environment: The external world, context, or substrate in which the agent operates and interacts.
  • Actuators: The hardware or software mechanisms through which the agent performs actions to manipulate or alter its environment.
  • Sensors: The physical instruments or digital inputs through which the agent perceives information and receives observations from the environment.

PEAS Specification for Automated Taxi Driver

An automated taxi represents a complex, dynamic, and high-stakes agent system. Its PEAS specification is detailed below:

  • Performance Measure: Safety (zero collisions), speed/punctuality, legal compliance (adherence to traffic rules), passenger comfort, and maximization of profit/fuel efficiency. Mathematically, the cumulative utility can be modeled as \( U = w_1 \cdot \text{Safety} + w_2 \cdot \text{Speed} + w_3 \cdot \text{Comfort} - w_4 \cdot \text{FuelCost} \).
  • Environment: City streets, highways, varied traffic conditions, weather conditions, pedestrians, road signals/signs, and passengers.
  • Actuators: Steering wheel, electronic throttle (accelerator), hydraulic brakes, turn signals, horn, display screen/speech synthesizer interface.
  • Sensors: LIDAR, RADAR, optical cameras, GPS receiver, wheel speed sensors, accelerometer, sonar proximity sensors, engine diagnostic sensors.

PEAS Specification for Medical Diagnosis System

A medical diagnosis agent operates as an expert diagnostic assistant in healthcare. Its PEAS specification includes:

  • Performance Measure: Patient health outcome optimization, diagnostic accuracy, minimization of false positives and false negatives, cost-effectiveness of recommended tests, and compliance with clinical protocols.
  • Environment: Patient health state, clinical history database, hospital laboratory system, medical staff, and diagnostic guidelines.
  • Actuators: Graphical interface displaying diagnosis reports, recommended clinical tests, medication prescriptions, and treatment plan suggestions.
  • Sensors: Keyboard/touchscreen for patient symptom entry, digital laboratory results, EHR (Electronic Health Record) data feeds, and direct vital sign monitoring instruments.

Overview of Agent Environment Classification

In Artificial Intelligence, the design of a rational agent is heavily constrained by the properties of its task environment. Environment classification determines the necessity of internal state tracking, probabilistic reasoning, real-time constraints, and strategic planning. Russell and Norvig categorize task environments along several orthogonal dimensions, of which the most fundamental are: Fully vs. Partially Observable, Deterministic vs. Stochastic, and Static vs. Dynamic.

1. Fully Observable vs. Partially Observable Environments

An environment is fully observable if an agent's sensors grant complete access to the complete state of the environment at any given point in time. Formally, if the sensor state \( O_t \) equals the true environment state \( S_t \) (i.e., \( O_t = S_t \)), the agent requires no internal memory to track world state. Examples include Chess and Crossword Puzzles.

Conversely, an environment is partially observable when sensory limits, noise, or unobservable factors prevent full state access (\( O_t = g(S_t) + \epsilon \)). The agent must maintain an internal state (e.g., belief state distributions) to keep track of unobserved aspects. Examples include Automated Driving (blind spots, hidden traffic) and Poker (opponent cards hidden).

2. Deterministic vs. Stochastic Environments

An environment is deterministic if the next state of the environment is completely determined by the current state and the action executed by the agent. Formally, the transition probability function satisfies \( P(S_{t+1} | S_t, a_t) = 1 \). If the environment is deterministic and fully observable, the agent faces no uncertainty. Examples include Eight-Puzzle and Sudoku.

An environment is stochastic if uncertainty exists regarding the next state due to random events, noise, or unpredictable dynamics, such that \( P(S_{t+1} | S_t, a_t) < 1 \). If the uncertainty arises from actions of other agents, it is termed strategic/adversarial. Examples include Ludo/Backgammon (dice rolls) and Automated Taxi driving.

3. Static vs. Dynamic Environments

An environment is static if it does not undergo change while the agent is deliberating or executing decision-making algorithms. The agent does not need to continuously monitor the world during thinking time, nor does it face time penalties for long deliberations. Examples include Sudoku and Crossword Puzzles.

A dynamic environment continuously changes state independently of the agent's actions while the agent deliberates. If an agent takes too long to decide, the state changes underneath it, rendering past observations stale. Examples include Automated Taxi driving and Robotic Soccer. If the environment state does not change with time but the agent's performance score decreases with time, it is classified as semistatic (e.g., timed Chess).

Overview of Uninformed Search Algorithms

Uninformed (Blind) Search Algorithms explore a state space relying solely on the problem definition (initial state, action set, transition model, and goal test) without using any domain-specific heuristic knowledge regarding the distance to the goal. These algorithms systematically generate search trees to find a sequence of actions leading from the initial state to a goal state.

1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Breadth-First Search expands the shallowest unexpanded node first. It is implemented using a Queue (FIFO) data structure for the search frontier. All nodes at depth \( d \) are expanded before any nodes at depth \( d+1 \).

  • Completeness: Complete if branching factor \( b \) is finite.
  • Optimality: Optimal if step costs are equal or uniform (cost is a non-decreasing function of depth).
  • Time Complexity: \( O(b^d) \), where \( b \) is the branching factor and \( d \) is the depth of the shallowest goal node.
  • Space Complexity: \( O(b^d) \), as all generated nodes remain stored in memory, making space the primary bottleneck.

2. Depth-First Search (DFS)

Depth-First Search expands the deepest unexpanded node first in the current search frontier. It is implemented using a Stack (LIFO) or recursive call stack.

  • Completeness: Incomplete in infinite-depth spaces or spaces with loops (can get trapped in infinite paths). Complete in finite state spaces with graph search (cycle detection).
  • Optimality: Non-optimal; it may return a very deep goal path when a much shallower goal exists.
  • Time Complexity: \( O(b^m) \), where \( m \) is the maximum depth of the state space.
  • Space Complexity: \( O(b \cdot m) \), offering linear memory consumption since it only stores nodes along the current path along with unexpanded siblings.

3. Depth-Limited Search (DLS)

Depth-Limited Search mitigates DFS's infinite-depth failure mode by enforcing an explicit depth limit \( l \). Nodes at depth \( l \) are treated as if they have no successors.

  • Completeness: Incomplete if the goal depth \( d > l \).
  • Optimality: Non-optimal if \( l > d \).
  • Complexity: Time complexity is \( O(b^l) \) and space complexity is linear \( O(b \cdot l) \).

4. Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search (IDDFS)

Iterative Deepening DFS repeatedly executes Depth-Limited Search while progressively increasing the depth limit from \( l = 0, 1, 2, \dots \) until a goal is discovered. It combines the space efficiency of DFS with the completeness and optimality guarantees of BFS.

Although states in top levels are regenerated across iterations, the computational overhead is minor because the number of nodes at depth \( d \) dominates the tree size. The total number of node expansions in IDDFS is given by:

\[ N(\text{IDDFS}) = (d+1)b^0 + d \cdot b^1 + (d-1)b^2 + \dots + 1 \cdot b^d = O(b^d) \]

Overview of A* Search Algorithm

A* Search is the most widely celebrated form of best-first search in Artificial Intelligence. It evaluates candidate search nodes by combining the proven path cost from the start state with an estimated heuristic cost to the goal. A* achieves optimal search efficiency by expanding the minimum necessary number of nodes required to guarantee an optimal path.

The Evaluation Function: \( f(n) = g(n) + h(n) \)

At any given node \( n \), A* evaluates its priority using the total cost estimation function:

\[ f(n) = g(n) + h(n) \]

Where each term represents:

  • \( g(n) \): The exact path cost incurred to reach node \( n \) from the initial state \( s_0 \). It guarantees that the search accounts for actual accumulated work.
  • \( h(n) \): The estimated cost of the cheapest path from node \( n \) to a goal state. This heuristic function incorporates domain-specific insight.
  • \( f(n) \): The estimated total cost of the cheapest solution path passing through node \( n \) from the initial state to a goal state.

Algorithmic Workflow

A* maintains two core data structures: an OPEN list (a priority queue ordered by ascending \( f(n) \)) and a CLOSED list (a set of previously expanded nodes to prevent cyclic redundancy). The complete execution pipeline functions as follows:

  1. Initialize OPEN with the start node \( s_0 \), setting \( g(s_0) = 0 \) and \( f(s_0) = h(s_0) \).
  2. Pop the node \( n \) with the minimum \( f(n) \) from OPEN.
  3. If \( n \) satisfies the goal test, terminate and return the extracted optimal path.
  4. Otherwise, move \( n \) to the CLOSED set and generate all valid successors \( n' \).
  5. For each successor \( n' \), compute tentative cost \( g_{\text{tentative}} = g(n) + c(n, a, n') \). If \( n' \) is unvisited or \( g_{\text{tentative}} < g(n') \), update parent pointers, record \( g(n') = g_{\text{tentative}} \), calculate \( f(n') = g(n') + h(n') \), and insert/update \( n' \) in OPEN.

Conditions for Optimality

The optimality of A* depends strictly on mathematical properties of the heuristic \( h(n) \):

  • Tree Search Optimality: Requires \( h(n) \) to be admissible (never overestimates true cost to goal, \( 0 \le h(n) \le h^*(n) \)).
  • Graph Search Optimality: Requires \( h(n) \) to be consistent (monotonic) (\( h(n) \le c(n, a, n') + h(n') \)), ensuring that \( f(n) \) is non-decreasing along any path.

Overview of Heuristic Conditions

In heuristic state-space search (specifically A* search), the performance, completeness, and optimality guarantees of the algorithm depend directly on formal mathematical constraints imposed on the heuristic evaluation function \( h(n) \). The two critical heuristic conditions are Admissibility and Consistency (Monotonicity).

1. Admissibility Condition

A heuristic function \( h(n) \) is defined as admissible if it never overestimates the true minimum cost required to reach a goal state from node \( n \). Admissibility implies that the heuristic is optimistic.

Formally, for all nodes \( n \):

\[ 0 \le h(n) \le h^*(n) \]

Where \( h^*(n) \) represents the true optimal path cost from node \( n \) to the nearest goal state \( G \), and by definition, \( h(G) = 0 \).

Significance of Admissibility

Admissibility is the necessary and sufficient condition for A* Tree-Search to guarantee finding an optimal solution. If \( h(n) \) were to overestimate the cost of an optimal path through node \( n \), A* might choose a suboptimal path whose estimated cost appears lower, discarding the true optimal solution.

2. Consistency (Monotonicity) Condition

A heuristic function \( h(n) \) is defined as consistent (or monotonic) if, for every node \( n \) and every successor \( n' \) generated by taking action \( a \), the estimated cost of reaching the goal from \( n \) is no greater than the step cost to \( n' \) plus the estimated cost to the goal from \( n' \).

Formally, for all nodes \( n \) and successors \( n' \):

\[ h(n) \le c(n, a, n') + h(n') \]

Where \( c(n, a, n') \) is the step cost of transitioning from \( n \) to \( n' \).

Monotonicity of \( f(n) \)

If \( h(n) \) is consistent, the total evaluation function \( f(n) = g(n) + h(n) \) is non-decreasing along any path:

\[ f(n') = g(n') + h(n') = g(n) + c(n, a, n') + h(n') \ge g(n) + h(n) = f(n) \]

Relationship Between Admissibility and Consistency

The relationship between these two theoretical guarantees is summarized as follows:

  • Consistency implies Admissibility: Every consistent heuristic is automatically admissible (proven via induction on path length to goal).
  • Admissibility does NOT imply Consistency: An admissible heuristic may violate triangle inequality locally, which in graph search could force node re-opening.
  • Graph Search Impact: Consistency is the prerequisite for A* Graph-Search to be optimal without requiring expensive path re-opening of closed nodes.

Overview of Hill Climbing Search

Hill Climbing Search is a fundamental local search algorithm that operates by iteratively moving in the direction of increasing value (or decreasing cost) to find an optimal state. It evaluates immediate neighbors of the current state and transitions to the neighbor offering the highest improvement. Because it retains only the current state in memory without maintaining a search tree, its memory complexity is remarkably efficient at \( O(1) \).

Hill Climbing is often described as a greedy local search because it grabs the best neighbor without considering future consequences or looking ahead beyond one step.

Algorithmic Workflow

  1. Evaluate the initial state \( s_{current} \).
  2. Loop: Generate all valid neighbor states of \( s_{current} \).
  3. Select the neighbor \( s_{best} \) with the maximum evaluation value \( f(s_{best}) \).
  4. If \( f(s_{best}) \le f(s_{current}) \), terminate and return \( s_{current} \) as the solution.
  5. Otherwise, set \( s_{current} = s_{best} \) and repeat.

Major Pitfalls of Hill Climbing

Due to its greedy local nature, basic Hill Climbing frequently fails to find global optima when operating on non-convex objective landscapes. The three classic failure modes are:

1. Local Maxima

A local maximum is a peak in the landscape higher than all its immediate neighbors, but lower than the global maximum. Once the agent reaches a local maximum, every neighboring state yields a lower evaluation score. The algorithm falsely concludes it has reached the optimal solution and gets stuck.

2. Ridges

A ridge is an elevated sequence of local maxima where the slope leads upward, but the orientation of the ridge runs diagonally across the grid of available moves. Because standard neighborhood operators only test axis-aligned single steps, every available step from a point on the ridge leads downward, causing search stagnation.

3. Plateaux and Flat Regions

A plateau is a flat region of the search space where adjacent states possess identical evaluation values (\( f(s_{neighbor}) = f(s_{current}) \)). On a plateau, the algorithm receives zero directional gradient signals, causing it to perform aimless random walks or terminate prematurely.

Remedial Strategies

  • Stochastic Hill Climbing: Randomly chooses among uphill moves, weighted by steepness.
  • Random-Restart Hill Climbing: Conducts repeated hill-climbing searches from randomly generated initial states, ensuring global coverage as number of restarts increases.
  • First-Choice Hill Climbing: Generates neighbors randomly until one is found that is strictly better than the current state.

Overview of Simulated Annealing

Simulated Annealing (SA) is a prominent probabilistic local search metaheuristic designed to locate global optima in complex, non-convex state spaces. Inspired by the metallurgical process of annealing—where metals are heated to high temperatures and slowly cooled to achieve low-energy, highly ordered crystalline structures—Simulated Annealing circumvents local maxima by deliberately permitting "downhill" (worse) moves under a controlled probabilistic regime.

Mathematical Mechanism and Acceptance Probability

At each step, SA evaluates a randomly chosen neighbor state \( s_{next} \). Let \( \Delta E = E(s_{next}) - E(s_{current}) \) represent the change in state value (for a maximization problem).

  • If \( \Delta E > 0 \) (the neighbor is superior), the algorithm accepts the move deterministically.
  • If \( \Delta E \le 0 \) (the neighbor is inferior), the algorithm accepts the move probabilistically according to the Boltzmann distribution:

\[ P(\text{accept}) = e^{\frac{\Delta E}{T}} \]

Where \( T \) is the system Temperature parameter. When \( T \) is extremely high, \( e^{\frac{\Delta E}{T}} \to 1 \), allowing the agent to perform an unrestricted random walk. As \( T \) approaches zero, \( e^{\frac{\Delta E}{T}} \to 0 \) for negative \( \Delta E \), causing SA to behave like pure, greedy Hill Climbing.

The Temperature Schedule

The performance and convergence of SA depend entirely on the cooling schedule \( T(t) \), which specifies how the temperature decreases over time step \( t \). Common schedule formulations include:

  • Exponential (Geometric) Decay: \( T_t = T_0 \cdot \alpha^t \), where \( 0.8 \le \alpha < 1.0 \). This is the most popular practical schedule.
  • Linear Decay: \( T_t = T_0 - \eta \cdot t \), where \( \eta \) is a constant cooling rate.
  • Logarithmic Decay: \( T_t = \frac{T_0}{\ln(1 + t)} \).

Theoretical Convergence Guarantee

According to the fundamental theorem of Simulated Annealing, if the temperature schedule decreases sufficiently slowly (such as under logarithmic decay), the probability of terminating at the global optimal state approaches 1:

\[ \lim_{t \to \infty} P(S_t \in \text{Global Optima}) = 1 \]

Overview of Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP)

In standard search algorithms, states are treated as atomic "black boxes." In contrast, a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) uses a factored representation where states are defined by a set of variables taking values from explicit domains. A solution to a CSP is a complete, consistent assignment of values to all variables such that no constraints are violated.

Formal Definition of CSP

Formally, a CSP is defined as a triple \( \langle X, D, C \rangle \):

  • Variables (\(X\)): A finite set of variables \( X = \{X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\} \).
  • Domains (\(D\)): A set of domains \( D = \{D_1, D_2, \dots, D_n\} \), where each domain \( D_i \) defines the set of allowable values for variable \( X_i \).
  • Constraints (\(C\)): A finite set of constraints \( C = \{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_m\} \). Each constraint \( C_i = \langle \text{scope}, \text{relation} \rangle \) specifies the subset of variables involved and the allowed combinations of values for those variables.

Formulation of the N-Queens Problem as a CSP

The classic N-Queens Problem requires placing \( N \) non-attacking chess queens on an \( N \times N \) chessboard such that no two queens share the same row, column, or diagonal.

The CSP formulation for N-Queens is defined as follows:

  • Variables: \( X = \{Q_1, Q_2, \dots, Q_N\} \), where variable \( Q_i \) represents the row position of the queen placed in column \( i \). (Assigning one queen per column automatically satisfies column constraints).
  • Domains: \( D_i = \{1, 2, \dots, N\} \) for all \( i \in \{1, \dots, N\} \).
  • Constraints: For every pair of distinct columns \( i \neq j \):
    • Row Constraint: \( Q_i \neq Q_j \) (No two queens in the same row).
    • Diagonal Constraint: \( |Q_i - Q_j| \neq |i - j| \) (No two queens on the same diagonal).

Binary vs. Non-Binary Constraints

Constraint Type Definition N-Queens Example
Unary Constraint Restricts the value of a single variable \( Q_1 \neq 2 \) (Queen 1 cannot be in row 2)
Binary Constraint Relates two variables \( Q_i \neq Q_j \) and \( |Q_i - Q_j| \neq |i - j| \)
Global/N-ary Constraint Involves an arbitrary number of variables \( \text{AllDifferent}(Q_1, Q_2, \dots, Q_N) \)

Overview of CSP Backtracking Search and AC-3

Solving Constraint Satisfaction Problems efficiently requires pairing a systematic search algorithm with continuous constraint propagation. The standard depth-first search for CSPs is Backtracking Search, which assigns values to one variable at a time and backtracks immediately upon encountering a constraint violation. Constraint propagation techniques like Arc Consistency (AC-3) prune illegal values from variable domains prior to or during search, drastically shrinking the state space.

Backtracking Search Algorithm & Heuristics

Backtracking Search builds a partial assignment tree. At each step, it picks an unassigned variable, iterates through its domain values, and recursively attempts to complete the assignment. Its efficiency is enhanced using domain-independent search heuristics:

  • Minimum Remaining Values (MRV / Fail-First): Chooses the variable with the fewest legal remaining values in its domain to fail early if an unsatisfiable branch is reached.
  • Degree Heuristic: Chooses the variable involved in the largest number of constraints on other unassigned variables (used as a tie-breaker for MRV).
  • Least Constraining Value (LCV): Chooses the value for a variable that rules out the fewest choices for neighboring variables in the constraint graph.

Arc Consistency and the AC-3 Algorithm

A directed arc \( (X_i, X_j) \) in a CSP constraint graph is defined as arc consistent if, for every value \( x \in D_i \), there exists at least one valid value \( y \in D_j \) that satisfies the binary constraint between \( X_i \) and \( X_j \).

AC-3 Algorithm Execution Procedure

  1. Initialize a queue \( Q \) containing all directed binary arcs \( (X_i, X_j) \) in the CSP.
  2. While \( Q \) is non-empty:
    • Pop arc \( (X_i, X_j) \) from \( Q \).
    • Call `Revise(CSP, Xi, Xj)` to remove any value \( x \in D_i \) for which no supporting value \( y \in D_j \) exists.
    • If `Revise` modifies domain \( D_i \):
      • If \( D_i \) becomes empty, return Failure (inconsistency detected).
      • Otherwise, insert all neighboring arcs \( (X_k, X_i) \) for all neighbors \( X_k \neq X_j \) back into \( Q \).
  3. Return Success (all remaining domains are arc consistent).

Complexity Analysis

For a CSP with \( n \) variables and maximum domain size \( d \):

  • Each arc \( (X_i, X_j) \) can be inserted into the queue at most \( d \) times because \( D_i \) has at most \( d \) values to delete.
  • With at most \( O(n^2) \) arcs, checking consistency of an arc takes \( O(d^2) \) time.
  • Total worst-case time complexity of AC-3 is \( O(n^2 d^3) \).

Overview of Game Playing and Adversarial Search

In Artificial Intelligence, game playing is modeled as an adversarial search problem. Unlike single-agent search algorithms where an agent seeks an optimal sequence of actions toward a static goal, adversarial search operates in competitive multi-agent environments where two or more players have opposing utility goals. The canonical setting involves two-player, deterministic, zero-sum games of perfect information (e.g., Chess, Checkers, Tic-Tac-Toe).

The Minimax Decision Rule

In a two-player zero-sum game, the players are designated as MAX (seeking to maximize the payoff utility) and MIN (seeking to minimize MAX's utility). The Minimax Value of any state \( n \) is computed recursively as follows:

\[ \text{Minimax}(n) = \begin{cases} \text{Utility}(n) & \text{if } n \text{ is a terminal state} \\ \max_{a \in \text{Actions}(n)} \text{Minimax}(\text{Result}(n, a)) & \text{if Player}(n) = \text{MAX} \\ \min_{a \in \text{Actions}(n)} \text{Minimax}(\text{Result}(n, a)) & \text{if Player}(n) = \text{MIN} \end{cases} \]

Algorithmic Mechanics of Minimax Search

The Minimax algorithm performs a complete depth-first exploration of the game tree down to terminal states:

  1. From the current state, MAX generates all legal moves and recursively calls Minimax on each successor node.
  2. At the next level down, MIN evaluates its legal responses, selecting the move that minimizes the resulting utility.
  3. Terminal utilities bubble up from the leaves to the root state. MAX then selects the move corresponding to the maximum child value.

Complexity and Optimality Properties

  • Time Complexity: \( O(b^m) \), where \( b \) is the legal branching factor and \( m \) is the maximum depth of the game tree.
  • Space Complexity: \( O(b \cdot m) \), since it performs a depth-first traversal storing nodes along the current search path.
  • Completeness: Complete if the game tree is finite.
  • Optimality: Optimal against an optimal opponent. If MIN plays sub-optimally, MAX achieves a score at least as high as the minimax value.

Enhancements: Alpha-Beta Pruning

Because expanding complete game trees to depth \( m \) is computationally intractable for games like Chess (\( b \approx 35, m \approx 100 \)), real-world adversarial search employs Alpha-Beta (\( \alpha \)-\( \beta \)) Pruning. By maintaining bounds \( \alpha \) (best choice for MAX so far) and \( \beta \) (best choice for MIN so far), branches that cannot possibly influence the final decision are pruned, reducing effective time complexity to \( O(b^{m/2}) \) under optimal move ordering.
